report.source_text: After the negative PCR results of the CSF acyclovir was stopped. The disturbances in fluid and electrolyte balance were treated with fluid resuscitation and potassium supplementation. Volume repletion was achieved quickly. The patient’s neurological status recovered within 36 hours after the start of ceftriaxone intravenously. Normalisation of sodium levels occurred within 24 hours and potassium levels normalised within 48 hours, after which fluid resuscitation was stopped.

clinician.current_trajectory_hypothesis: 45-year-old MSM with acute S. flexneri gastroenteritis complicated by toxic encephalopathy with secondary electrolyte derangement. Stool culture confirmed S. flexneri (ceftriaxone-sensitive). CSF showed mild pleiocytosis with normal glucose/protein. Blood cultures negative, ruling out bacteremia/sepsis. Treatment with IV ceftriaxone and fluid/electrolyte resuscitation led to rapid neurological recovery within 36 hours and normalization of electrolytes within 24-48 hours. The encephalopathy appears to have been primarily driven by hyponatremia and/or hyperkalemia secondary to the acute gastroenteritis.

report.source_text: Three days after admittance to the hospital and the start of intravenous antibiotic treatment, the patient had recovered so far that he could be discharged. The stool consistency returned to normal over time. Because of subsiding symptoms in a non-immunocompromised patient, no further antibiotic treatment was found necessary. At a follow-up visit several weeks later, he had recovered fully, except for some memory problems.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 45-year-old MSM with recent unprotected sexual contact presented to the emergency department with acute onset fever (39.5°C), diarrhea, and encephalopathy (lethargy, confusion, disorientation, diminished speech) with hemodynamic compromise (BP 100/50 mmHg, HR 104/min). Stool culture on admission identified Shigella flexneri (ceftriaxone-sensitive, fluoroquinolone-resistant). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleiocytosis (8×10^6 cells/L) with normal glucose and protein, ruling out bacterial meningitis. Blood cultures remained negative and lactate was normal, excluding sepsis. Admission electrolytes showed mild hyponatremia (130 mmol/L) and hypokalemia (3.4 mmol/L), though these were deemed insufficient to fully explain the neurological status. CT brain showed no cerebral bleeding or hydrocephalus. The patient was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and fluid/electrolyte resuscitation. Neurological status recovered completely within 36 hours, electrolytes normalized within 24-48 hours, and stool consistency returned to normal. The patient was discharged on hospital day 3 without further antibiotic treatment. At follow-up several weeks later, he had recovered fully except for some residual memory problems.
